r1-across-1.statement: The base's long-answer failures (low-temperature loops, cap hits, inability to continue its own long prefix) come from early-to-mid-layer self-copying of its own earlier reasoning by induction-driven repeat circuitry (attention heads from layer 7 and repeat-reading MLP neurons in layers 10-15), and the cap-hit part of RL's gain is a diffuse, task-general weakening of that self-copy pathway in layers 0-15, which temperature, restarts and an RL-written prefix each partly substitute for.

r1-across-2.statement: The 10-13 points that Olmo-3.1 RL holds over the cued base are mostly a learned token-budget controller, trained by 3.1's scoring of truncated rollouts as failures, that keeps self-checking ('Wait') on answers that are short for the budget and forces convergence before the 16k cap on long ones, written into the weights as a low-rank late-layer stop/deliberation readout; it is not new mathematical skill, so the gap sits in cap hits and long problems, every recovering transplant takes RL's length, and Olmo-3.0 RL (truncation masked) is close to the cued base.

r1-all-1.statement: The cued base and Olmo-3.1 RL-Zero-Math have nearly the same per-step math skill; the residual gap is a long-horizon self-conditioning deficit, in which the base's next-token distribution degrades as its own generated solution grows (loops at T 0.6, unfinished drift at T 1.0). Olmo-3.1's RL, which trained truncated rollouts as negatives at 16k, repaired this with a diffuse weight direction that changes activations only deep inside long math contexts, so the gap scales with solution length and token budget, not with problem knowledge.

r1-all-2.statement: Most of the RL-Zero-Math gain is a saturating answer-mode switch: deliberate, then box the answer and stop, never the base's 'Answer:' line. The switch is encoded redundantly along one diffuse direction spread over every layer and matrix, so any unbiased fraction of the delta (half the matrices, a DARE 1 % sample, or a small multiple a of the whole delta) flips it. Accuracy is therefore a sharply concave function of delta scale; the cue flips the same switch from the prompt, and other RL runs (Code-RL) share part of it.

r1-surprises-2.statement: The functional part of the RL-Zero-Math weight change is a low-rank, near-linear shift (a few coherent singular directions per matrix, dense across neurons, that write a deliberation/answer-format readout into the residual stream), while the high-rank remainder that holds most of the change energy is optimizer noise that does almost nothing; so neuron subsets fail (each holds only its proportional share of the dense low-rank part), DARE works (it preserves the low-rank part in expectation and adds only high-rank noise), and RL leaves neuron features unchanged on general text.

r2-across-1.statement: The RL-Zero-Math weight change acts, to first order, as a logit shift that collapses next-token entropy only at the base's own high-entropy fork positions and leaves low-entropy positions alone, so the RL model carries a fork-local low temperature: global temperature barely moves RL because its forks are already near one-hot, whereas for the base, cooling to T 0.6 also sharpens the easy restatement step at diffuse forks and starts loops, and heating to T 1.0 removes loops but samples wrong branches at the forks; any partial delta (attention-only, MLP-only, a times the delta) collapses fork entropy partly and stays temperature-sensitive in proportion to the fork entropy it leaves.

r2-across-2.statement: The RL-Zero-Math delta is small (0.24 % of weight norm) and sign-coherent: its function lies in the joint sign pattern of many coordinates, whose Fisher curvature on the base's own math samples is hundreds to thousands of times that of a random direction of the same norm, not in its large entries. So the effect of any edit is its energy divided by that leverage. Random resampling (DARE), random-sign or random-direction edits of the same norm, and magnitude-ranked subsets add almost nothing beyond their unbiased share of the sign pattern. The model's activations on general text barely move. The dose curve stays near-linear past a = 1. DARE fails only when its noise energy (1-q)/q exceeds the leverage, which puts the cliff at q of about 0.01-0.05 %. A large, low-coherence SFT delta (bytegraft, Think-SFT) fails all of these tests.

r2-all-1.statement: The RL-Zero-Math delta acts through the coherent sign pattern of its entries along high-curvature (high on-policy Fisher) directions, roughly 700 times more consequential per unit norm than a random direction, and not through which entries are large; so any unbiased resampling of it (DARE, either half of the tensors) keeps the gain until the injected noise's KL, about (1-q)/(q*rho) times the delta's own, outgrows it, magnitude-ranked neurons do no better than random ones, the same magnitudes with random signs do nothing, and a low-leverage imitation (SFT) delta breaks under the same sparse copy.

r2-all-2.statement: The base's accuracy at a sampling setting is set by the per-token surprise of the text it generates relative to one optimum: below it, a restatement that holds its probability in one sequence beats a progress step whose mass is split over many paraphrases and then self-reinforces into a loop (boredom trap), above it the text drifts (confusion trap); the opening cue moves the base into a lower-entropy deliberative mode, which is why the cue loops more than the plain prompt at T 0.6, is worth far more at T 1.0, and why any mode-sharpening truncation (top-p < 1) costs the cued base but helps the plain base at T 1.0.

r2-external-1.statement: On Olmo-3 the RL-Zero-Math delta moves the output about 700 times more per unit of weight energy than a random direction does, because its signs are coherent, so DARE's rescaling noise costs at most about the delta's own KL down to q = 0.1 % and the plateau must end in a sharp cliff near q = 0.01 %; within that range the noise acts on generation as a small fixed random logit distortion that raises the surprise of generated text and so weakens self-reinforcing repetition: random-sign weight noise reduces loops and adds accuracy on a looping model at T 0.6 and costs a little at T 1.0, where there are no loops to break.

r2-external-2.statement: The cued base's two temperature failure modes come from one global temperature acting on two kinds of positions: at its rare high-entropy fork tokens the progress continuations split their mass while one restatement of an earlier step keeps its own, so T 0.6 or top-p 0.95 hands the fork to the restatement and starts a self-reinforcing loop, while at its many near-deterministic tokens T 1.0 samples tail tokens that become slips; RL sharpens the fork tokens onto one progress continuation and lowers entropy elsewhere, which is why it is temperature-insensitive, and a per-position temperature (1.0 at forks, 0.6 elsewhere) gives the base the loop-free finishing of T 1.0 and the finished-answer accuracy of T 0.6.

r2-revise-1.statement: The accuracy-carrying part of the Olmo-3.1 RL-Zero-Math delta is its dense sign pattern over many small entries, which moves logits to first order as a coherent sum with high Fisher leverage per unit norm; magnitudes, the most-changed entries and the low-rank head (top singular directions) carry only their proportional share of it, so an arm recovers accuracy in proportion to how much of the coherent sign pattern it keeps in expectation (per-problem log-odds roughly linear in that share), DARE survives until its scaled noise breaks the network, sign randomization gives nothing, and the Code-RL pattern, which agrees with Math-RL in sign at chance, gives no math gain.

r2-revise-2.statement: The cued base's remaining gap to RL-Zero-Math is a weak error detector, not weaker per-step math: both models make slips and misreads in a first candidate solution at similar rates, but RL notices an error and re-derives far more often (signal-detection d' about 1.1 vs 0.6), so the cued base's residual errors are sample-specific commitment errors that independent samples rarely repeat while RL's residual errors are problem-specific; hence a 4-sample majority vote closes about half of the cued base's gap but lifts RL by only about 1 point, an injected error in a shared prefix is caught far more often by RL, and any RL-Zero-Math release (3.0 included) gives finished answers far more accurate than the cued base's, whatever its cap-hit rate.

r2-surprises-1.statement: For the Olmo-3 base, loops and slips are the two ends of one axis, the per-token surprise of the text it samples (low surprise: the boredom trap of self-reinforcing repetition; high surprise: the confusion trap of compounding slips and early wrong stops); the opening cue lowers the base's native per-token entropy by selecting its reasoning-trace register, which pushes it toward loops at T 0.6 (more cap hits than the plain base) and keeps it out of confusion at T 1.0 (where the plain base loses 28 points on short problems), while the entropy-collapsed RL policy sits far from both traps and so ignores temperature, and any change that raises the base's surprise, including a random weight perturbation, cuts its loops.

r2-surprises-2.statement: Which entries the RL-Zero update moves, and by how much each, is set by the base and the optimizer rather than by the task (Adam gives every consistently signed coordinate a near-equal step, and bf16 storage registers a step only where it exceeds half an ulp of |w|), so the changed-entry mask and entry magnitudes carry almost no task information; the task is written only in the signs, and their effect is gated by which input directions the processed text excites, so RL changes the computation on any math-solution text whoever wrote it and leaves general text untouched.
